supports.locator: Direct expansion through three recursive products

claims.statement: The recurrence T(n)=3T(n/2)+O(n) solves to O(n^log2(3)), approximately O(n^1.585).

learner.audience: Undergraduate computer-science learners meeting divide-and-conquer multiplication for the first time.

criteria: Explains why the cross term needs no fourth recursive multiplication
objectives.statement: Derive the three-product identity from place-value expansion.
Apply the method to 1234 × 5678 and recombine exactly.
Compare Karatsuba and grade-school asymptotic multiplication costs.

provenance.notes: All narrative and source material is locally authored; external DOI is reviewer context only.

purpose: Flagship twelve-minute fixture for grounded pedagogy, exact mathematics, scene-local regeneration, captions, sources, and multi-target rendering.

qualityAssertions.description: All required worked-example values remain exact.
Every externally verifiable claim has entailing or supporting evidence.
Editing the example narration leaves unrelated source and complexity scene artifacts byte-identical.
Captions stay within safe areas and never cover equations or intermediate values.
All declared targets render deterministically in the canonical environment.
Blind reviewer mean for accuracy, sequence, visual explanation, audio, and usability.

scenes.accessibilityDescription: A diagram changes from four multiplication links to three, with labels read in order.
scenes.captionText: Can four smaller products become three?
scenes.narration: A direct split seems to need four smaller multiplications. Karatsuba finds the same cross term with only three.
scenes.title: Can four products become three?
scenes.visualIntent: Two two-digit blocks split into a, b, c, d; four product links collapse into three highlighted links.

scenes.accessibilityDescription: The equation expansion is read step by step, ending with the derived middle coefficient.
scenes.narration: Expand place values, then compute z two, z zero, and one combined product. Subtract the outer products to isolate a d plus b c.
scenes.title: Build the identity
scenes.visualIntent: Semantic equation segments transform in discrete, reduced-motion-safe steps.

scenes.accessibilityDescription: A four-row arithmetic table lists the split, three products, middle term, and final recombination.
scenes.narration: Split at two digits. The three products are 672, 2652, and 6164. Their adjusted middle is 2840, and recombination gives 7,006,652.
scenes.title: Work 1234 × 5678
scenes.visualIntent: Place-value columns keep all intermediate values visible and align the final addition.

scenes.accessibilityDescription: Two labeled growth curves show Karatsuba rising more slowly than quadratic multiplication.
scenes.narration: Three half-size recursive products yield n to log base two of three, about n to 1.585, versus quadratic grade-school multiplication.
scenes.title: Why three matters
scenes.visualIntent: Log-scale curves and recurrence trees use labels and line patterns in addition to color.

scenes.accessibilityDescription: A numbered five-step recap links the method to the completed example.
scenes.captionText: Split → three products → middle term → recombine → compare
scenes.narration: Split, compute the two outer products and one sum product, recover the middle, and recombine by place value.
scenes.title: Three products, one recombination
scenes.visualIntent: A five-step concept thread revisits the exact example without introducing new claims.

title: Karatsuba Multiplication: Three Products Instead of Four
